questions.question: A decoder has 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128 and fp16 values (2 bytes). How many bytes of KV cache does one token take?
questions.explanation: Bytes per token = 2 × L × H_kv × d × b = 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes (128 KiB). The factor 2 counts one key and one value vector. Lesson 54.1 uses this same configuration.

questions.question: Using the same configuration (131,072 bytes per token), how many tokens fit in a 16 GiB KV cache?
questions.explanation: 16 GiB = 16 × 2^30 bytes, and 16 × 2^30 / 131,072 = 131,072 tokens. Lesson 54.1 prints this value in its first code block.

questions.question: Blocks hold 16 tokens. A request has a 40-token prompt. How many blocks does the prompt need, and in which logical block and offset does token 37 sit (counting from 0)?
questions.explanation: ceil(40/16) = 3 blocks. Token 37 is in logical block floor(37/16) = 2 at offset 37 − 32 = 5. Its physical block is whatever the block table maps logical block 2 to; the lesson's example maps it to physical block 9.

questions.question: In the Lesson 54.1 simulation (200 requests, 8,192 KV slots, 2,048-token reservation), what fraction of KV memory held real tokens under reserve-the-maximum allocation, and under paged allocation?

options.text: about 22% under reservation and about 98% under paging
about 98% under reservation and about 22% under paging
about 60% under reservation and about 95% under paging
about 22% under reservation and about 100% under paging

questions.explanation: The simulation prints utilization=0.219 for the contiguous (reserve-maximum) run and utilization=0.983 for the paged run. Paging also costs 305 preemptions that discard 3,777 tokens, which must be generated again.

questions.question: Six requests with 3, 8, 2, 5, 4 and 6 output tokens run on three slots. Static batching takes 14 steps and continuous batching takes 13. Both produce 28 tokens. Why is continuous batching faster here?

options.text: It produces more tokens per request than static batching
It refills a slot as soon as its request ends, so fewer slots sit idle
It skips the prefill step for short requests
It holds every request in a fixed group until the longest one finishes

questions.explanation: Static batching waits for the whole group before taking new requests, so slots that finish early sit idle. Continuous batching re-decides the batch at every step. The two schedules produce the same 28 tokens, and the trace in Lesson 54.1 shows the 14-step and 13-step schedules.

questions.question: A fused kernel reads x and r and writes y, each an 8 × 4096 fp16 tensor. The unfused three-kernel chain moves 7 tensor passes. What is the ratio of unfused to fused memory traffic?
questions.explanation: S = 8 × 4096 = 32,768 values. Unfused traffic is 7S × 2 = 458,752 bytes. Fused traffic is 3S × 2 = 196,608 bytes. The ratio is 7/3 ≈ 2.333, which Lesson 54.2 prints. This counts bytes only; run time is not measured.

questions.question: A Triton config declares max_batch_size: 8. An input has a per-request shape of 1024 features. Which dims value is correct?
questions.explanation: The Triton model configuration documentation says dims excludes the batch dimension. Triton adds the batch dimension from max_batch_size, so including 8 or 1 in dims gives a second batch dimension.

questions.question: A script calls Ollama's /api/generate with the default settings and reads the answer from response["text"]. Which is the correct way to get the answer as one JSON object?

options.text: Read response["response"] and send "stream": false in the request

questions.explanation: The text is in the response field, and /api/generate streams by default, so the request must set "stream": false to get a single object. Lesson 54.3 lists both mistakes as traps.
